name: Identity & access (IAM)
summary: Who can do what, to which resource.
howItWorks: Identity and access management authenticates every caller (people, services, machines) and checks each API call against policies. Cloud IAM denies by default: a request succeeds only if some policy explicitly allows that action on that resource and no policy explicitly denies it. The goal is least privilege, where each identity has exactly the permissions its job needs.
analogy: Keycards in an office building. Your card opens the doors your job needs, and every swipe is logged.
useWhen: Every cloud account, from day one
Giving services short-lived role credentials instead of long-lived keys
Separating what developers, CI and production workloads can touch
avoidWhen: One shared admin login for several people or services
example: A report function’s role allows `s3:GetObject` on `reports/*` and nothing more. When an intern’s account tries to delete objects in that bucket, the call fails with AccessDenied.

diagram.caption: Three identities call the same bucket. Policy evaluation allows the function role and the CI pipeline their specific actions, and denies the intern’s delete by default.

story: Access control used to be managed one user at a time: administrators wrote access control lists that spelled out, for each person, what they could touch. In a large organisation that was slow and costly. In 1992 Ferraiolo and Kuhn at the US National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) published a formal model for role-based access control (RBAC): permissions belong to roles that match job functions, and people are given roles. It became an ANSI standard in 2004, and by 2010 most users at organisations with more than 500 employees were on RBAC systems.

Cloud computing turned every server, bucket and database into an API, and every API call needed an authorization decision. AWS launched Identity and Access Management in 2011 with JSON policy documents that allow specific actions on specific resources under conditions, and deny everything else. Federation and short-lived credentials soon followed, and OAuth 2.0, published in 2012, standardised how an application gets limited access to another service on a user’s behalf.

In 2014 Google described BeyondCorp, which dropped the idea of a trusted internal network: every request is checked against the user and the device, wherever it comes from. Identity, rather than network location, became the main security boundary, and today workloads and CI jobs increasingly prove who they are with short-lived tokens instead of stored passwords and keys.

choices.choice: Grant permissions to roles, not individuals
choices.why: Listing permissions for each user individually didn’t scale. Tying permissions to roles means a new hire, a transfer or a departure is one change, and it is easier to see who can do what.
A request succeeds only if a policy explicitly allows it, so a forgotten rule fails closed. That is what makes least privilege, granting only what a job needs, enforceable.
Perimeter security meant that once an attacker got inside the network, they had relatively easy access to everything. Checking each request’s user and device removes that soft interior.
A password or access key that never expires is valuable when it leaks. Temporary credentials, from AWS’s 2011 federation tokens to OIDC tokens for CI jobs, expire on their own.

timeline.text: Ferraiolo and Kuhn formalise role-based access control at NIST
AWS IAM launches with JSON policies; federation follows in August
Google’s BeyondCorp paper drops the trusted internal network
Google’s Zanzibar handles trillions of ACLs for Drive, YouTube and more
GitHub Actions jobs get short-lived cloud credentials via OIDC
